---
title: "Walkthrough: from weekly spend to a budget recommendation"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "100%", dpi = 110)
options(digits = 4)
```

This article follows one question from raw data to an answer: if the
marketing budget stays the same, should any of it move between channels?
It uses the north geography of `mm_weekly`, 156 weeks of five channels,
generated from known parameters so that every step can be checked against the
truth.

The getting-started vignette, `vignette("mediamix")`, introduces each
function. This article is about using them together, and about where the
answer is solid and where it is not.

The setup keeps the parameters `mm_weekly` was generated from in `truth`, and
adds a week counter to serve as the trend control:

```{r}
library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)

channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
north <- north[order(north$date), ]
north$week <- seq_len(nrow(north))
```

## 1. Check the data can answer the question

A model can only tell channels apart if they move independently of one
another and vary from week to week. `diagnose_media()` checks both before
anything is fitted:

```{r}
d <- diagnose_media(north, media = channels, decay = 0.6)
d
d$collinearity[, c("channel", "vif", "most_correlated_with", "correlation")]
```

`decay = 0.6` measures collinearity after a representative adstock, since
smoothed series correlate more than raw spend and the model sees the smoothed
ones. No channel is collinear enough to make its coefficient meaningless: the
largest variance inflation factor (`vif`) is
`r round(max(d$collinearity$vif), 2)`, well under `diagnose_media()`'s
default warning level of 5. Every channel varies, but video and display are
dark, with no spend at all, in
`r round(100 * d$variation$zero_share[d$variation$channel == "video"])`% and
`r round(100 * d$variation$zero_share[d$variation$channel == "display"])`% of
weeks, so they carry less information than their row count suggests, which is
worth remembering when their numbers come out.

## 2. Carryover: how well does the data identify it?

Tune every channel's carryover at once, in one model that also holds the
controls, so no channel is credited with another's effect or with the trend:

```{r}
controls <- north[c("week", "price", "seasonality", "holiday")]
grid <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)

joint <- tune_carryover_joint(north[channels], north$revenue,
                              controls = controls, decays = grid)
rbind(truth  = truth$decay[channels],
      best   = joint$best$decay,
      one_se = joint$best_1se$decay)
```

`best` is the minimum of each channel's cross-validation curve, and `one_se`
the shortest carryover within one standard error of it. The curves themselves
show how firmly the data pins each decay down:

```{r fig.height = 5.5}
plot(joint, truth = truth$decay)
```

Television, social and display land within 0.1 of the truth and video within
0.2. Search does not, and its profile says why: it is nearly flat, so the data
holds almost no information about search's carryover. For search the
one-standard-error choice falls back to a short carryover, which here is close
to right; for every other channel it is shorter than the truth.

The joint search does not tune saturation. To keep this walkthrough about the
*decision* rather than the estimation, the rest of it uses the generating
parameters, which is what a full joint search over carryover *and*
saturation, as in `vignette("tidymodels")`, is trying to reach. Section 7
comes back to what happens when television's carryover is uncertain.

## 3. Fit the model

The model is ordinary least squares on the transformed media and the
controls. `spec` holds each channel's carryover and saturation.
`transform_plan()` applies them to any spend plan and returns the plan with
each channel's column transformed, so section 7 can reuse `spec` on budgets
that were never run:

```{r}
spec <- lapply(channels, function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
names(spec) <- channels

media <- transform_plan(north, spec)[channels]
model_data <- cbind(media, controls)
fit <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = model_data)
round(rbind(estimate = coef(fit)[channels], truth = truth$beta[channels]))
```

Even with the transforms right, the coefficients land well away from the
truth: search's is
`r round(100 * (1 - coef(fit)[["search"]] / truth$beta[["search"]]))`% too
low and social's
`r round(100 * (coef(fit)[["social"]] / truth$beta[["social"]] - 1))`% too
high. That is three years of weekly noise, and section 8 shows what it does to
the answer.

## 4. Where did the revenue come from?

`contributions()` splits each week's fitted revenue into one part per channel
and a baseline, and `roi()` divides each channel's total contribution by its
total spend to give its average return:

```{r}
contrib <- contributions(media, fit, index = north$date)
avg <- roi(contrib, north[channels])
avg
```

Every channel returns more than it costs on average. On this table alone the
tempting move is to take money from television, the lowest average ROI, and
give it to social, the highest.

## 5. What would the next pound do?

Average ROI describes the budget that was spent. The reallocation question is
about the *margin*, and `marginal_roi()` answers it by re-running the whole
transform on a slightly larger budget. Given the plan, the coefficients and
`spec`, it does every channel at once, and its `roi` column is the average
return from section 4:

```{r}
marginal <- marginal_roi(north, coef(fit), spec = spec)
marginal[order(-marginal$mroi), c("channel", "mroi", "roi", "spend")]
```

The ranking changes. Social still has the highest marginal return, but
television is no longer at the bottom: its S-shaped response means its next
pound works nearly as hard as its average one. Display is now last, and its
estimated marginal return is below 1: in this model, the last pounds spent on
it did not pay for themselves.

The chart sets each channel's average return (open circle) beside its
marginal return (filled circle); the vertical line is break-even:

```{r avg-vs-marginal, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8}
ink <- mm_palette(role = "ink")
cols <- mm_palette(2)
o <- marginal[order(marginal$mroi), ]
op <- par(mar = c(4, 6, 1, 1), bg = ink[["surface"]], fg = ink[["axis"]])
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, max(o$roi) * 1.05), ylim = c(0.5, nrow(o) + 0.5),
     yaxt = "n", bty = "n", xlab = "Revenue per pound", ylab = "",
     col.axis = ink[["muted"]], col.lab = ink[["secondary"]])
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(o)), labels = o$channel, las = 1, lwd = 0,
     col.axis = ink[["secondary"]])
abline(v = 1, col = ink[["muted"]])
text(1, nrow(o) + 0.45, "break-even", pos = 4, cex = 0.75, col = ink[["muted"]])
segments(o$mroi, seq_len(nrow(o)), o$roi, seq_len(nrow(o)),
         col = ink[["axis"]], lwd = 2)
points(o$roi, seq_len(nrow(o)), pch = 21, bg = ink[["surface"]], col = cols[1],
       cex = 1.6, lwd = 2)
points(o$mroi, seq_len(nrow(o)), pch = 21, bg = cols[2],
       col = ink[["surface"]], cex = 1.6, lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("average", "marginal"), pch = 21,
       pt.bg = c(ink[["surface"]], cols[2]), col = c(cols[1], ink[["surface"]]),
       pt.cex = 1.4, bty = "n", text.col = ink[["secondary"]])
par(op)
```

So in this model the candidate move is *display to social*, not *television
to social*.

## 6. How sure are we?

Every number so far is a point estimate from one sample of 156 weeks. A block
bootstrap resamples runs of consecutive weeks, refits the model, and
recomputes, which shows how much of the ranking survives sampling noise. The
transform is not re-run on the resampled rows, because that would glue
unrelated weeks together and carry spend across the joins. Each replicate
refits the coefficients on resampled rows and recomputes average and marginal
return on the original spend plan:

```{r}
boot_data <- cbind(revenue = north$revenue, media, controls)

returns <- function(d) {
  f <- lm(revenue ~ ., data = d)
  r <- marginal_roi(north, coef(f), spec = spec)
  out <- c(rbind(r$roi, r$mroi))
  names(out) <- paste(rep(r$channel, each = 2), c("average", "marginal"),
                      sep = ": ")
  out
}

boot <- block_bootstrap(boot_data, returns, times = 200, block_length = 13,
                        seed = 2026)
boot
```

```{r boot-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(boot, reference = 1, xlab = "Revenue per pound")
```

The intervals are wide. Only the intervals for
`r knitr::combine_words(boot$term[boot$lower > 1], before = "\x60", oxford_comma = FALSE)`
lie entirely above break-even; every other interval crosses 1, and both of
display's reach below zero. They hold the transforms at the true parameters
chosen in section 3, so they show sampling uncertainty in the coefficients
only. Two channels' intervals overlapping does not settle a comparison between
them, because their estimates move together from replicate to replicate, so
ask the paired question directly:

```{r}
reps <- attr(boot, "replicates")
paired <- c(social_beats_display = mean(reps[, "social: marginal"] >
                                          reps[, "display: marginal"]),
            social_beats_tv      = mean(reps[, "social: marginal"] >
                                          reps[, "tv: marginal"]))
paired
```

Social's marginal return beats display's in
`r round(100 * paired[["social_beats_display"]])`% of replicates and
television's in `r round(100 * paired[["social_beats_tv"]])`%. That is the
honest strength of the evidence for moving money into social: more likely
right than wrong, and not more than that. It is a reason to run the move as a
test, not to announce it.

## 7. Test the move before recommending it

A marginal return is a derivative. A real reallocation is a finite change, and
the response curves bend along the way, so simulate the new plan through the
model rather than multiplying by a marginal rate. `reallocate()` builds the new
plan, keeping each channel's flighting: it takes the amount from one channel
in proportion to its spend in each week and adds it to the other in
proportion to that channel's. `simulate_plan()` runs a plan through `spec` and
the coefficients, and with `baseline` it adds each channel's change in spend
and in predicted response. Everything except the two channels is held fixed,
and the controls do not change, so the sum of `response_change` is the
difference in predicted revenue:

```{r}
tenth <- 0.10 * sum(north$display)
to_social <- reallocate(north, from = "display", to = "social",
                        amount = tenth)
simulate_plan(to_social, spec, coef(fit), baseline = north)
```

The same two steps compare several moves, here by the gain per pound moved:

```{r}
move <- function(from, to, amount, spec, coefficients = coef(fit)) {
  plan <- reallocate(north, from = from, to = to, amount = amount)
  change <- simulate_plan(plan, spec, coefficients, baseline = north)
  gain <- sum(change$response_change)
  c(moved = amount, revenue_change = gain, per_pound_moved = gain / amount)
}

rbind(
  `display -> social` = move("display", "social", tenth, spec),
  `tv -> social`      = move("tv", "social", tenth, spec),
  `display -> social, 2.5x` = move("display", "social", 2.5 * tenth, spec)
)
```

In the model, moving a tenth of display's budget into social raises predicted
revenue at no extra cost. Moving the *same amount* out of television instead,
the move the average-ROI table suggested, gains less, because it gives up
television's still-steep fitted response. Moving two and a half times as much
out of display gains more in total but less per pound, as social climbs its
own curve.

Two checks before this goes in a deck. First, is the new plan inside the data?

```{r}
peak <- function(amount) {
  max(reallocate(north, from = "display", to = "social",
                 amount = amount)$social)
}
c(observed = max(north$social), smaller_move = peak(tenth),
  larger_move = peak(2.5 * tenth))
```

Both moves push social's busiest week above anything in the data: the smaller
by about `r round(100 * (peak(tenth) / max(north$social) - 1))`%, the larger
by about `r round(100 * (peak(2.5 * tenth) / max(north$social) - 1))`%. A
little beyond the observed range is the unavoidable price of asking what
*more* would do, but the further out a plan goes, the more of its predicted
gain is the fitted curve's shape rather than evidence. The smaller move stays
close enough to the data to be worth testing; the larger one should wait for
that test.

Second, how sensitive is the answer to carryover it could not pin down? In
section 2 the data was consistent with a television decay as low as the
one-standard-error value. Refit with that, and compare television's marginal
return and the display-to-social move under the two fits:

```{r}
tv_alt <- joint$best_1se$decay[joint$best_1se$channel == "tv"]
spec_alt <- spec
spec_alt$tv$adstock$decay <- tv_alt

media_alt <- transform_plan(north, spec_alt)[channels]
fit_alt <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = cbind(media_alt, controls))

tv_mroi_alt <- marginal_roi(north, coef(fit_alt), spec = spec_alt["tv"])$mroi
sensitivity <- rbind(
  true_decay   = c(tv_decay = truth$decay[["tv"]],
                   tv_mroi = marginal$mroi[marginal$channel == "tv"],
                   display_to_social = move("display", "social", tenth,
                                            spec)[["per_pound_moved"]]),
  one_se_decay = c(tv_decay = tv_alt,
                   tv_mroi = tv_mroi_alt,
                   display_to_social = move("display", "social", tenth, spec_alt,
                                            coef(fit_alt))[["per_pound_moved"]])
)
sensitivity
```

Television's marginal return depends heavily on a carryover the data only
loosely identifies: at the shorter decay its next pound no longer pays for
itself. The display-to-social move does not touch television's budget, but it
is not immune either, because refitting moves display's and social's
coefficients too: it still gains, but
`r round(sensitivity["one_se_decay", "display_to_social"], 2)` per pound moved
rather than `r round(sensitivity["true_decay", "display_to_social"], 2)`. Its
direction survives a carryover the data cannot rule out, which makes it the
cleaner test; its size does not. Whether television is over- or under-funded
is a question this data cannot settle, and saying so is part of the answer.

The moves so far were chosen by hand. `allocate_budget()` asks what the fitted
model would do with the whole budget: how to split the same total across all
five channels so that predicted media response is as large as possible.

```{r allocation, fig.height = 3.6}
best <- allocate_budget(north, spec, coef(fit))
best$allocation[, c("channel", "current_spend", "recommended_spend", "mroi")]
plot(best)
```

It rescales each channel's whole series, so every channel keeps its flighting
and only its total changes. It works out each channel's predicted response at
every multiple of a step, here
`r format(round(best$step), big.mark = ",")`, and picks the combination that
spends the whole budget with the largest predicted response. On the fitted
model that takes money from television, video and display and puts most of
it into social. At the recommended split the channels' marginal returns all lie
between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(best$allocation$mroi))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(best$allocation$mroi))`, against
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(marginal$mroi))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(marginal$mroi))` now.

The allocation works from point estimates. It takes the coefficients and
`spec` as exact, so read it together with section 6, where social's marginal
return beat display's in
`r round(100 * paired[["social_beats_display"]])`% of replicates and
television's in `r round(100 * paired[["social_beats_tv"]])`%, and with the
carryover check above: it cuts television, the channel that check could not
call either way. It also goes where the data does not, raising social's
busiest week to `r format(round(max(best$plan$social)), big.mark = ",")`,
`r round(100 * (max(best$plan$social) / max(north$social) - 1))`% above
anything observed. It is the fitted model's best split on that grid, and,
like the moves above, a hypothesis to test.

## 8. Check the answer against the truth

`mm_weekly` was simulated, so this decision can be checked against the
parameters that generated it, which a real analysis never can. The same
marginal returns and moves, with the true coefficients in place of the fitted
ones:

```{r}
true_returns <- marginal_roi(north, truth$beta, spec = spec)
true_mroi <- stats::setNames(true_returns$mroi, true_returns$channel)
round(rbind(fitted = stats::setNames(marginal$mroi, marginal$channel),
            truth = true_mroi), 2)

true_per_pound <- function(from, to, amount) {
  move(from, to, amount, spec, truth$beta)[["per_pound_moved"]]
}
true_moves <- c(`display -> social` = true_per_pound("display", "social", tenth),
                `tv -> social`      = true_per_pound("tv", "social", tenth),
                `tv -> search`      = true_per_pound("tv", "search", tenth))
round(true_moves, 2)

# The allocation from section 7, and the best split under the truth
best_true <- allocate_budget(north, spec, truth$beta)
gain <- function(allocation, coefficients) {
  sum(simulate_plan(allocation$plan, spec, coefficients,
                    baseline = north)$response_change)
}
allocation_gain <- c(predicted = gain(best, coef(fit)),
                     in_truth = gain(best, truth$beta),
                     best_in_truth = gain(best_true, truth$beta))
round(allocation_gain)
```

The direction of the display-to-social move holds up: it raises revenue in
truth too. Everything else this analysis concluded about the ranking does not.
The fitted model overstates that move's gain per pound about
`r round(move("display", "social", tenth, spec)[["per_pound_moved"]] / true_moves[["display -> social"]], 1)`-fold,
and in truth television has the lowest marginal return
(`r round(true_mroi[["tv"]], 2)`) and search the highest
(`r round(true_mroi[["search"]], 2)`), so the best move takes from television,
the channel this analysis could not call either way, and gives to search.
The allocation fares the same way. Its split still gains in truth, but
`r format(round(allocation_gain[["in_truth"]]), big.mark = ",")` rather than
the `r format(round(allocation_gain[["predicted"]]), big.mark = ",")` the
fitted model predicted, while the split that is best under the true
parameters would gain
`r format(round(allocation_gain[["best_in_truth"]]), big.mark = ",")`.

No step above was a mistake of method. Three years of weekly noise moved the
coefficients enough to reorder channels whose true returns sit within a few
tenths of each other, which is what the wide intervals in section 6 and the
`r round(100 * paired[["social_beats_display"]])`% paired probability were
saying. A real analysis has no truth to check against, which is why the next
section treats the result as a hypothesis.

## 9. What to say, and what not to

The analysis supports a test, not a reallocation. The fitted model points at
moving around a tenth of display's budget into social; the bootstrap puts the
odds of that ranking at roughly
`r round(100 * paired[["social_beats_display"]])` in 100; and section 8 shows
how a fitted model can misrank channels whose returns are close. Run the move
as a geo experiment: change the allocation in one region, compare it with the
others, and use the measured result to calibrate the model's priors or
constraints. Leave television's budget alone until its carryover is better
measured, in either direction.

`reallocate()` sets up the test plan: with `by = "geo"` and an amount named by
region, it moves spend in that region only.

```{r}
test_plan <- reallocate(mm_weekly, from = "display", to = "social",
                        amount = c(north = tenth), by = "geo")
tapply(test_plan$social - mm_weekly$social, mm_weekly$geo, sum)
```

What this analysis does not support: a precise revenue forecast for the new
plan, any move that takes a channel far outside the spend it has historically
run at, or a ranking of channels by average ROI, or by marginal ROI without a
test.
